'''Patricia Fara''' is a college lecturer in the history of science at [[Clare College, Cambridge]]. She is a graduate of the [[University of Oxford]] and did her PhD at the [[University of London]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/03/19/books/review/lab-of-ones-own-patricia-fara-broad-band-claire-evans.html|title=Science's Invisible Women|last=Sobel|first=Dava|date=2018-03-19|work=The New York Times|access-date=2019-01-17|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> She is a former Fellow of [[Darwin College, Cambridge|Darwin College]] and is an Emerita Fellow of [[Clare College]], where she was previously Director of Studies in the History and Philosophy of Science.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.clare.cam.ac.uk/fellows-and-staff-directory/pf10006/ |title=Clare College Fellows, referenced 28 November 2016 |access-date=12 March 2015 |archive-date=20 November 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161120004712/http://www.clare.cam.ac.uk/Fellows-and-Staff-Directory/pf10006/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> Fara was also a College Teaching Officer in the [[Department of History and Philosophy of Science, Cambridge|Department of History and Philosophy of Science]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.people.hps.cam.ac.uk/index/affiliates/fara |title=Department of the History and Philosophy of Science, Cambridge, referenced 28 November 2016 |access-date=28 November 2016 |archive-date=28 November 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161128195442/http://www.people.hps.cam.ac.uk/index/affiliates/fara |url-status=dead }}</ref> From 2016 to 2018, Fara was President of the [[British Society for the History of Science]]. In 2016, she became President of the Antiquarian Horological Society.<ref name=":1">{{Cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/money/2017/jun/07/keep-women-in-academia-by-providing-childcare-cambridge-university-historian-urges-universities|title=Keep women in academia by providing childcare, historian urges universities|first=Ian |last=Sample |date=2017-06-07|newspaper=The Guardian|access-date=2019-01-17|language=en-GB|issn=0261-3077}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|date=2016|title=The new President|url=https://ahsoc.contentfiles.net/media/assets/file/The_New_President__wm6.pdf|journal=Antiquarian Horology|volume=37|issue=2|page=178|archive-date=4 December 2019|access-date=4 December 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191204075908/https://ahsoc.contentfiles.net/media/assets/file/The_New_President__wm6.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref> Fara is author of numerous popular books on the history of science and has been a guest on [[BBC Radio 4]]'s science and history discussion series ''[[In Our Time (BBC Radio 4)|In Our Time]]''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.bshs.org.uk/patricia-fara-on-in-our-time|title=Patricia Fara on In Our Time|last=Moulds|first=Alison|date=2018-02-15|website=The British Society for the History of Science (BSHS)|language=en-US|access-date=2019-01-17}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Fara began her career as a physics teacher but returned to graduate studies as a mature student to specialise in [[History and Philosophy of Science]], completing her [[PhD]] thesis at [[Imperial College]], London, in 1993.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Baldwin |first=Melinda |date=2018-08-10|title=Q&A: Patricia Fara on the British women scientists who broke barriers|journal=Physics Today|issue=8 |language=EN|doi=10.1063/PT.6.4.20180810a|s2cid=240330712 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Fara|first=Patricia|date=1993|title=Magnetic England in the 18th Century|url=https://www.history.ac.uk/history-online/theses/thesis/magnetic-england-18th-century|journal=PhD Thesis, London|archive-date=17 April 2019|access-date=17 January 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190417201238/https://www.history.ac.uk/history-online/theses/thesis/magnetic-england-18th-century|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Research and writing==
Her areas of particular academic interest include the role of portraiture and art in the history of science, science in 18th-century England during the [[Age of Enlightenment|Enlightenment]], and the role of women in science. She has written about numerous women in science, mathematics, engineering and medicine, including: [[Hertha Ayrton]], [[Lady Helena Gleichen|Lady Helen Gleichen]], [[Mona Chalmers Watson]], [[Helen Gwynne-Vaughan]], [[Isabel Emslie Hutton]], [[Flora Murray]], [[Ida Maclean]], [[Marie Stopes]], and [[Martha Annie Whiteley]].<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.chemistryworld.com/features/science-suffrage-and-misogyny/3009589.article|title=Science, suffrage and misogyny|date=10 December 2018|first=Rachel |last=Brazil|website=Chemistry World|language=en|access-date=2019-01-17}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.the-scientist.com/reading-frames/book-excerpt-from-a-lab-of-ones-own-30022|title=Book Excerpt from A Lab of One's Own|website=The Scientist Magazine®|language=en|access-date=2019-01-17|archive-date=26 June 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200626011851/https://www.the-scientist.com/reading-frames/book-excerpt-from-a-lab-of-ones-own-30022|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://theconversation.com/helena-gleichen-pioneer-radiographer-suffragist-and-forgotten-hero-of-world-war-i-124367|title=Helena Gleichen: pioneer radiographer, suffragist and forgotten hero of WWI|last=Fara|first=Patricia|date=November 8, 2019|website=The Conversation|access-date=December 29, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.sciencefocus.com/science/helen-gwynne-vaughan-an-extraordinary-botanist-whose-problems-of-identity-still-confront-female-scientists-today/|title=Helen Gwynne-Vaughan: An extraordinary botanist whose problems of identity still confront female scientists today|first=Patricia|last=Fara|website=BBC Science Focus Magazine|language=en|date=8 March 2020|access-date=2019-12-29}}</ref> Fara has argued for expanded access to childcare as a means of increasing the retention of women in science.<ref name=":1" /> She has written and co-authored a number of books for children on science. Fara is also a reviewer of books on history of science.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://literaryreview.co.uk/watchers-of-the-skies|first=Patricia |last=Fara |title= Watchers of the Skies|website=Literary Review|date=October 2008|language=en|access-date=29 December 2019}}</ref> She has written the award-winning ''Science: A Four Thousand Year History'' (2009)<ref name=":2">Fara, Patricia (2009) ''Science: A Four Thousand Year History'' Oxford: Oxford University Press</ref><ref>Ferry, Georgina (2009) [https://www.theguardian.com/books/2009/apr/25/science-patricia-fara-review 'Under the January 2018|url=https://www.theguardian.com/books/2018/jan/03/lab-ones-own-science-suffrage-first-world-war-patricia-fara-review |title=A Lab of One's Own: Science and Suffrage in the First World War by Patricia Fara review – trailblazing feminist'|newspaper=The Guardian}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last=Bruton|first= Elizabeth |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-018-00109-2 |title=When Suffragettes kicked open the lab door|journal=Nature|date= 10 January 2018|volume= 553 |issue= 7687 |page= 154 |doi= 10.1038/d41586-018-00109-2 |pmid= 32094765 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite magazine|url=https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2018/05/21/the-overstory-theory-of-bastards-a-lab-of-ones-own-and-a-mouth-is-always-muzzled|title=Briefly Noted Book Reviews|magazine=[[The New Yorker]]|date=14 May 2018 |language=en|access-date=2019-12-29}}</ref> In 2013, Fara published an article in the journal [[Nature (journal)|''Nature'']], stressing the fact that biographies of female scientists perpetuate stereotypes.''<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Fara|first=Patricia|date=2013-03-06|title=Women in science: Weird
